n: James, a leader of the early Church in Jerusalem and the Lord’s brother, writes to believing Jews scattered across the Roman world. He calls himself simply a servant, not boasting of his family tie to Jesus.

f.g: Traditionally James the brother of the Lord, not James the son of Zebedee.
Greek diaspora — Israelites living outside the Holy Land.

n: James opens with a surprising command: treat hard trials as a reason for joy. He does not mean trials feel good, but that God can use them for our growth.

f.g: divers = various; temptations here means trials of every kind. The JST reads ‘many afflictions.’

n: The reason for joy: when faith is tested, it produces endurance. Like a muscle under strain, faith grows stronger by being tried.

f.g: Greek hypomonē — steady endurance, staying power under pressure.

n: Let endurance finish its work. The goal is to become whole and mature—complete in character, not lacking anything God wants us to become.

f.g: Greek teleios — complete, mature, fully developed.
wanting = lacking.

n: This is the verse that sent fourteen-year-old Joseph Smith into the woods to pray in 1820. James promises that God gives wisdom generously to anyone who asks and never scolds them for asking.

f.g: upbraid = scold or reproach; God does not shame us for asking.

n: The asking must come with real trust. A person who keeps flip-flopping is like ocean surf pushed back and forth by the wind—never settled in one direction.

f.g: Not doubting; not divided between trust and distrust.

n: Someone who prays while privately expecting nothing should not be surprised to receive nothing. Faith is the channel through which God’s answers come.
A “double minded” person has two souls pulling in opposite directions. Divided loyalty makes a person unsteady in every part of life, not just in prayer.

f.g: Greek dipsychos — literally ‘two-souled.’

n: James turns to rich and poor. The poor believer can rejoice because, in Christ, he is lifted up and made an heir of God’s kingdom.

f.g: Humble or poor in worldly standing.

n: The rich believer should rejoice in being humbled, because wealth is as short-lived as a wildflower. Recognizing that keeps him honest about what really lasts.
James paints a scene from Palestine: the hot sun and dry east wind can wither the fields in a day. Wealth fades just as fast, even while the rich man is busy with his plans.

f.g: Possibly the scorching east wind (sirocco) that withers vegetation.
The beauty of its appearance.

n: The one who endures testing faithfully is truly happy. Like a victorious athlete, he will receive a crown—here, eternal life—promised to those who love God.
Don’t blame God for temptations to do evil. God is untouched by evil and never lures anyone into sin.

f.g: God allows us to be tested, but He never entices anyone toward sin.

n: Temptation comes from inside us—our own desires drag us away and bait the hook. James uses fishing and hunting images for being lured.

f.g: Strong desire of any kind, not only sexual desire.
Literally ‘baited,’ like luring a fish.

n: James traces sin’s life cycle like a birth: desire conceives, gives birth to sin, and sin, fully grown, gives birth to death. Stopping temptation early stops the whole chain.
A short, loving warning: don’t be deceived about where evil and good come from.
Everything truly good comes from God, the Creator of the heavenly lights. Unlike the sun and moon, which shift and cast moving shadows, God never changes.

f.g: God as creator of the sun, moon and stars.

n: God chose to give us new spiritual birth through the gospel message. We are like the first and best of the harvest, offered to Him.

f.g: The first part of a harvest, dedicated to God under the law of Moses.

n: James gives timeless counsel: listen quickly, speak slowly, and be slow to anger. It is simple advice for families, friendships, and online life alike.
Human anger doesn’t produce the kind of right living God wants. Getting angry rarely makes anything holier.
So strip off moral filth and the overflow of wickedness, and humbly welcome God’s word, which can take root inside you and save you.

f.g: An overflow or excess of wickedness; naughtiness = evil.
The word ‘implanted’ or rooted in you, like a seed.

n: Hearing the gospel is not enough; we must act on it. Those who only listen are fooling themselves about where they stand.
James compares a listener who doesn’t act to someone glancing in a mirror. Ancient mirrors were polished metal and gave only a dim reflection.

f.g: A mirror, usually polished bronze in that day.

n: He looks, walks away, and immediately forgets what he saw. Gospel truth shows us who we really are, but it only helps if we remember and change.
By contrast, someone who looks closely into God’s law and keeps living it will be blessed in what he does. God’s law is called the law of liberty because it frees us.
Outward religion means little if a person can’t control his speech. An unbridled tongue shows that someone is fooling himself about his devotion.

f.g: Like a horse without a bridle—uncontrolled.
Empty, worthless.

n: James defines true religion in practical terms: care for orphans and widows in their struggles, and stay morally clean in a corrupt world.
